opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think my students are just as good. Sometimes I even think they're better in certain ways, though it's a different kind of "good."

When I was at Facebook AI Research, and from what I see at places like Google DeepMind or OpenAI, the researchers are incredibly strong. They're experienced and efficient, and they have access to enormous compute and very mature infrastructure. They know how to get a big project over the finish line. That's something students usually can't match, at least not at first.

But what I value most in my students is something else. They're hungry, and they're willing to take risks. A PhD student doesn't have a product roadmap or a quarterly goal hanging over them. They can spend months on a question that looks a bit crazy, one that may not work out at all. In a big lab, even a very good researcher often has to align with the company's priorities, and that naturally narrows what they're willing to explore.

The other thing is that students haven't been "trained" too much by the system yet. They don't carry as many assumptions about what's supposed to work. Some of the most interesting ideas in our group came from a student asking a question that a more senior person would have dismissed as naive. Often that naive question turns out to be the right one.

Of course, there's a gap in engineering maturity and in resources. Part of my job as an advisor is to help close that gap: teaching them how to run experiments rigorously, how to write, and how to tell a coherent research story. But in terms of raw talent, curiosity and taste, I really don't think there's a fundamental difference. And I'd go further. Academia's role right now isn't to compete with industry labs on scale. It's to do the things they can't or won't do. For that, I think my students are exactly the right people.

r001.rationale: The candidate says leading-lab researchers are more experienced and describes a gap in engineering maturity; it does not say any students are more mature than those researchers.

r002.rationale: The candidate says students have a gap in engineering maturity and resources, not stronger engineering ability than leading-lab researchers.

r003.rationale: The candidate says there is no fundamental difference in raw talent, curiosity, and taste; it does not claim students have better research taste.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: That's a question I get asked a lot, and I think my honest answer is that the gap is much smaller than people assume, and the gap that does exist is mostly not about talent.

When I was at FAIR, I worked alongside people who were extremely strong, and I think the thing that made them strong wasn't raw intelligence. It was taste, and it was compute, and it was the environment. If you put a good student next to a thousand GPUs and a team of people who have spent five years thinking about the same problem, they will look like a genius very quickly. That's just what happens when you remove friction.

So when I look at my students at NYU, what I see are people who are just as smart, often more hungry, but who are operating with maybe one or two percent of the resources. And I actually think that constraint is a feature, not a bug, at least for the kind of research I care about. If you can't brute-force your way to an answer, you have to think harder about the question. A lot of my students' best work, things like the work on self-supervised learning or the Cambrian work on multimodal models, came out of the fact that we simply could not afford to train the obvious thing, so we had to find the non-obvious thing.

The place where I do see a real difference is in what I'd call research maturity. People at top labs have usually already made their mistakes. They know which ideas are dead ends, they know how to read a loss curve and tell within an hour whether something is working. Students are still building that intuition, and my job is basically to compress that timeline for them. I try to give them a lot of freedom but also be very honest, sometimes brutally honest, about which directions I think are going nowhere.

And one more thing I'd say. The industry lab researchers are extremely good at execution, but they are often working on what the organization needs. My students get to work on what they genuinely find interesting, and over a long horizon I think that produces a different kind of researcher. Some of the people I'm proudest of are the ones who went into these labs and brought that independent mindset with them, rather than the other way around.

r001.rationale: The candidate says researchers at top labs have greater research maturity and students are still building intuition; it does not say any students are more mature than lab researchers.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes industry lab researchers as extremely good at execution, but does not say any students have stronger engineering ability than lab researchers.

r003.rationale: The candidate attributes strong researchers' performance partly to taste, but does not say any students have better research taste than lab researchers.

astra-6.text:
I think the strongest students can absolutely do work at the level of researchers in leading labs. The difference is often experience rather than ability. An experienced researcher usually has a better sense of which questions are worth pursuing, which experiments will be informative, and when to stop going down a particular path. Students are still developing that judgment.

But that can also be an advantage. They haven’t internalized all the assumptions about what should or shouldn’t work, so they may try something that a more experienced person would dismiss. As an advisor, I want to help them develop good judgment without taking away that willingness to explore.

So I wouldn’t simply rank students against researchers at a lab. I’d look at how independently they think, how quickly they learn from a failed experiment, and whether they’re starting to ask questions that surprise me. That’s a much more meaningful signal.

r001.rationale: The candidate says students are still developing judgment and does not say any student is more mature than every researcher encountered at leading labs.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the strongest students can work at the level of leading lab researchers, but makes no claim that any student has stronger engineering ability than all of them.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses developing judgment about which questions to pursue, but does not say any student has better research taste than every researcher encountered at leading labs.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be careful about ranking them on a single scale. Students are still developing their research taste: which questions matter, what evidence to trust, and when to keep pushing versus change direction. Experienced researchers at strong labs have usually had more opportunities to develop that judgment.

But students can be just as capable of producing an important insight. They may question an assumption that someone more experienced takes for granted. So I don’t think of the difference as a fixed gap in ability. My job is to give students enough support—and enough independence—to develop their own judgment and surprise me.
